altText: Navy slide with Educate Me AI logo. Text: GCSE and A-level, mocks season. What to revise when you can’t revise everything. A quick way to pick what comes first.

Sort it in 10 minutes. 1: List what’s in the mock. Ask your teacher what each mock covers; not every topic will be in it. 2: Rate each topic: confident, getting there, or not yet. 3: Start in the middle. Getting there topics first: you already know some of it, so a little practice goes a long way.

Then make each session count. Questions first: try a question before you re-read your notes. Mix it up: two or three subjects a day, in short blocks. Not yet: for not yet topics, learn the basics, key words, definitions and the main ideas.

Short on time for a topic? Two cards. Learn the key words, enough to understand the question and start an answer. Practise one exam-style question, then check it against the answer and fix one thing. Mocks are practice. Whatever you don’t get to goes on your list for afterwards.

posts.title: Series circuits: what stays the same?
posts.planGate: Metricool Free plan: schedule only after Rej has confirmed the Starter upgrade in chat
altText: Reel, Lock It In number 4, GCSE Physics, Electricity. Question: in a series circuit, what’s the same and what’s shared? Two cards side by side. Current: the same through each component, measured in amps, for example 0.2 A at every point. Potential difference, also called voltage, in volts: shared across the components, for example a 6 V supply giving 2 V plus 4 V. Text: Current, one loop, so the same current flows through every component. Potential difference, the supply’s p.d. is shared between the components. Resistance, add them up, total R equals R1 plus R2. Memory trick: series, current stays, p.d. splits. Parallel is the other way round: same p.d. on each branch, the current splits. Ends on: Save this. Lock it in. Follow for Lock It In number 5.

platforms.label: Instagram Reel
platforms.caption:
Series circuits at GCSE: there’s one loop, so the current is the same through every component. The potential difference (voltage) of the supply is shared between the components, so a 6 V supply could give 2 V across one and 4 V across the other. And the total resistance is the resistances added up.

Memory trick: series, current stays, p.d. splits. Parallel is the other way round: the same p.d. across each branch, and the current splits between branches.

posts.planGate: Metricool Free plan: schedule only after Rej has confirmed the Starter upgrade in chat
altText: Navy slide with Educate Me AI logo. Text: For parents, mocks season. Mocks this term or in January? Schools choose their own dates. How to find out, and what helps either way.

Finding out. Check the school’s newsletter, website, app or parent portal; mock dates are often posted there. Ask your teenager what’s on and when; a shared calendar helps. Mocks are set by the school, not the exam board, so dates and subjects differ from school to school.

Either way. The Christmas break looks a bit different. Mocks before Christmas: a proper break, results may come back in January. Mocks in January: a little, not a lot, a light plan over the holidays with real days off. Make the plan together, so it’s theirs.

In mocks week. Space: a quiet spot to revise, and somewhere to keep the timetable. Routine: keep evenings normal, meals together, downtime and a sensible bedtime. Mocks are practice. The results are a to-do list, not a verdict.

altText: Navy slide. Question of the day. GCSE Maths, AQA, Edexcel and OCR, Foundation and Higher, Ratio, 3 marks. In a class, 15 students walk to school. The ratio of students who walk to students who don’t is 3 : 5. How many students are in the class? Original practice question by Educate Me AI, not from a past paper.
Have a go first. Comment your answer, then swipe to check. Hint: which number in the ratio does the 15 go with?

The answer: 40 students. How marks are usually given: 1 mark for one part, 15 divided by 3 equals 5; 1 mark for counting the parts, 3 plus 5 equals 8, or 5 times 5 equals 25 who don’t walk; 1 mark for 8 times 5 equals 40, or 15 plus 25 equals 40. The 15 is one share, not the whole class, so don’t start with 15 divided by 8.
